Towards Disentangled Preference Optimization Dynamics
Beyond Likelihood Displacement

Wei Chen Affiliation: South China University of Technology    Yubing Wu Affiliation: South China University of Technology    Junmei Yang Affiliation: South China University of Technology    Delu Zeng Affiliation: South China University of Technology Correspondence to: dlzeng@scut.edu.cn    Qibin Zhao Affiliation: AIP, RIKEN    John Paisley Affiliation: Columbia University    Min Chen Affiliation: South China University of Technology    Zhou Wang Affiliation: University of Waterloo
Abstract

Preference optimization is widely used to align large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. However, many margin-based objectives suppress the chosen response along with the rejected one, a phenomenon known as likelihood displacement, and no general mechanism currently prevents this across objectives. We bridge this gap by presenting a unified incentive-score decomposition of preference optimization, revealing that diverse objectives share identical local update directions and differ only in their scalar weighting coefficients. Building on this decomposition, by analyzing the dynamics of the chosen/rejected likelihoods, we identify the disentanglement band (DB), a simple, testable condition that characterizes when training can avoid likelihood displacement by realizing the preferred pathway: suppressing the loser while maintaining the winner, possibly after an initial transient. Leveraging the DB, we propose a plug-and-play reward calibration (RC) that adaptively rebalances chosen versus rejected updates to satisfy the DB and mitigate likelihood displacement, without redesigning the base objective. Empirical results show that RC steers training toward more disentangled dynamics and often improves downstream performance across a range of objectives. Our code is available at https://github.com/IceyWuu/DisentangledPreferenceOptimization.

1 Introduction

Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences has shifted from online reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) pipelines (Christiano et al., 2017; Bai et al., 2022; Ouyang et al., 2022) to stable offline optimization. Direct preference optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023) catalyzed this shift by reframing alignment as a classification problem (Xiao et al., 2025), spawning a wide family of objectives that improve efficiency (Tang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024a), mitigate length bias (Park et al., 2024; Meng et al., 2024), and incorporate constraints (Xu et al., 2024a; Azar et al., 2024).

However, increasing the preference margin alone does not determine how the chosen and rejected likelihoods move. Ideally, training suppresses the rejected response without degrading the chosen one, which we formalize as Pathway (iii) (Sec. 3.1). In contrast, many margin-based objectives entangle these updates, where suppressing the loser also drags down the winner, causing likelihood displacement (Razin et al., 2025) and exhibiting gradient entanglement (Yuan et al., 2025), the squeezing effect (Ren and Sutherland, 2025), and 3D-properties (Yan et al., 2025).

Some recent objectives treat the chosen and rejected terms more asymmetrically, often motivated by density ratio estimation (Sugiyama et al., 2012). In our diagnostics (e.g., Fig. 2(a)), objectives such as DIL (Xiao et al., 2025), DDRO (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025), and BPO (Kim et al., 2025) more often avoid the lockstep winner–loser drift seen in margin-based objectives. We refer to this regime as disentangled dynamics (vs. entangled dynamics of margin-based objectives). Yet these objectives are often discussed as distinct families, leaving a broader question open:

What objective property governs the induced likelihood dynamics, and how can we steer training toward Pathway (iii) even for entangled objectives?

We address this with an incentive-score decomposition. Regardless of objective form, the gradient update decomposes along the same score directions; objective design mainly enters through two scalar incentives that weight them (Tab. 1). This yields a continuous-time analysis (Sec. 3.2) and a simple, testable condition—the disentanglement band (DB)—that characterizes when training can enter Pathway (iii) (Tab. 2), possibly after an initial transient.

Finally, we translate this condition into a plug-and-play intervention. We propose reward calibration (RC), which adaptively rebalances chosen vs. rejected updates to make Pathway (iii) more likely, without redesigning the base objective (overview in Fig. 1). RC often steers training toward the Pathway (iii) regime across objectives and model scales (see Figs. 4 and C.5), with gains that transfer to downstream benchmarks (see Tabs. 4 and C.4).

To summarize, our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    We introduce an incentive-score decomposition that applies to both entangled margin-based and disentangled density ratio-based objectives, isolating scalar incentives as the key control variables (Tab. 1).

  2. 2.

    We derive likelihood dynamics and identify the DB, a simple, testable condition that characterizes when training can avoid likelihood displacement and realize the desired Pathway (iii) regime.

  3. 3.

    We propose a plug-and-play RC wrapper that rebalances chosen vs. rejected updates to mitigate likelihood displacement and promote Pathway (iii) across diverse objectives, without redesigning the base objectives.

  4. 4.

    We empirically verify that RC improves likelihood dynamics across objectives and model scales, often improving downstream alignment on benchmarks and in open-ended evaluation (Tab. 4, Sec. C.4).

2 Related Works and Background

2.1 Related Works

LLM Alignment: From PPO to a Zoo of Objectives.

For a long time, aligning LLMs with human preferences meant relying on the standard RLHF pipeline: train a reward model, then optimize the policy using PPO (Christiano et al., 2017; Schulman et al., 2017; Bai et al., 2022; Ouyang et al., 2022). In practice, however, getting PPO to work reliably is tough. It is computationally expensive and notoriously sensitive to hyperparameters (Engstrom et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2023). Consequently, the field shifted toward offline methods that skip the explicit reward modeling step. DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) really kicked this door open, framing alignment as a stable classification problem.

Since then, numerous DPO variants have been proposed. Some address specific issues such as length bias (e.g., SimPO (Meng et al., 2024), R-DPO (Park et al., 2024)), while others introduce constraints to limit model drift (e.g., CPO (Xu et al., 2024a), IPO (Azar et al., 2024)). Additional work targets better sample efficiency (Tang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024a), robustness against noisy data (Chowdhury et al., 2024) and diverse LLM architectures and efficiency techniques (Li et al., 2024c; Li et al., 2025c; Li et al., 2026). Yet, while we have plenty of new objectives, we often lack a clear and unified picture of what they are actually doing to the model’s internal probability updates.

Entangled vs. Disentangled Objectives.

Broadly, preference optimization objectives fall into two categories. The first, and currently dominant, class relies on an entangled margin derived from the Bradley–Terry assumption (Bradley and Terry, 1952), as exemplified by DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023), IPO (Azar et al., 2024), and CPO (Xu et al., 2024a). By coupling the chosen and rejected likelihoods through a single margin, these objectives limit asymmetric control (Yuan et al., 2025). As a result, suppressing the rejected likelihood often also depresses the chosen one, leading to phenomena such as the likelihood displacement (Razin et al., 2025) and gradient entanglement (Yuan et al., 2025).

This limitation has motivated a newer line of work explicitly decouples winner and loser rewards. Such disentanglement appears in methods for unpaired data, such as KTO (Ethayarajh et al., 2024), as well as in density ratio-based objectives. For example, DIL (Xiao et al., 2025) is derived from imitation learning bounds, while DDRO (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025) and BPO (Kim et al., 2025) build on statistical consistency and Bregman divergences (Bregman, 1967; Sugiyama et al., 2012). By disentangling chosen and rejected rewards, these methods enable asymmetric control over updates, often yielding more stable and selective suppression of rejected responses.

Interpretability of Preference Optimization and Learning Dynamics.

Proposing a new objective is one thing; explaining why it succeeds or fails during optimization is another. Recent work has increasingly sought to interpret preference optimization by examining its assumptions and learning dynamics. Some studies question the rigidity of the Bradley–Terry assumption (Azar et al., 2024; Munos et al., 2024; Ethayarajh et al., 2024) or analyze the impact of noisy preference labels (Chowdhury et al., 2024), while others focus on downstream pathologies such as length bias exploitation (Park et al., 2024), reward over-optimization (Gao et al., 2023), and likelihood displacement relative to the reference model (Razin et al., 2025; Pal et al., 2024).

Most closely related are dynamical analyses of preference optimization. Ren and Sutherland (2025) study likelihood shifts during fine-tuning, while Yuan et al. (2025) identify gradient entanglement in margin-based objectives. Although continuous-time dynamics have been used more broadly (Li et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2024b), existing work remains fragmented: margin-based objectives are analyzed dynamically, whereas density ratio methods (e.g., BPO (Kim et al., 2025), DIL (Xiao et al., 2025), DDRO (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025)) are not. We bridge this gap by unifying entangled and disentangled objectives under a common dynamical framework via incentive-score decomposition.

Entangled Margin-Based Objectives.

For a given triplet (𝒙,𝒚w,𝒚l)({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{w},{\bm{y}}_{l}), a broad class of margin-based preference objectives adopt a entangled template (Yuan et al., 2025):

ℒ⁡(zw,zl)=ℓ⁡(hw​(zw)−hl​(zl)−c)+Λ⁡(zw),\mathcal{L}(z_{w},z_{l})=\ell\left(h_{w}(z_{w})-h_{l}(z_{l})-c\right)+\Lambda(z_{w}), (1)

where ℓ⁡(⋅)\ell(\cdot) is an outer shaping function, hwh_{w} and hlh_{l} are transformations, cc is a constant offset, and Λ⁡(zw)\Lambda(z_{w}) is an optional chosen-only term, e.g., a likelihood regularizer in SlicHF (Zhao et al., 2023). Margin-based variants can be interpreted as instantiations of Eq. 1 by setting different ℓ\ell, hwh_{w}, hlh_{l}, cc, and Λ\Lambda (see Sec. A.3 for details).

In this case, DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) is an entangled objective with ℓ⁡(⋅)=−log⁡σ⁡(⋅),hw|l​(zw|l)=β​zw|l\ell(\cdot)=-\log\sigma(\cdot),h_{w|l}(z_{w|l})=\beta z_{w|l}:

ℒDPO​(zw,zl)=−log⁡σ⁡(β⁡(zw−zl−zwref+zlref)),\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}(z_{w},z_{l})=-\log\sigma\left(\beta\left(z_{w}-z_{l}-z_{w}^{\text{ref}}+z_{l}^{\text{ref}}\right)\right), (2)

where β>0\beta>0 is a hyperparameter, zwrefz_{w}^{\text{ref}} and zlrefz_{l}^{\text{ref}} are constants for a given reference model πref\pi_{\text{ref}} and triplet (𝒙,𝒚w,𝒚l)({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{w},{\bm{y}}_{l}).

3 Disentanglement Band and Plug-and-Play Reward Calibration

In this section, we analyze preference optimization through training-time likelihood dynamics. Motivated by empirical differences between entangled and disentangled objectives, we study how objective structure shapes likelihood trajectories and enables the desired behavior, and how this analysis yields a simple, practical way to steer these dynamics.

3.1 Unifying Objectives via Incentives

The Three Pathways of Margin Growth.

Under the Bradley-Terry assumption, most alignment objectives aim to increase the preference margin m=zw−zlm=z_{w}-z_{l}. However, a larger margin is a scalar outcome that can be achieved via three qualitatively distinct pathways in the (zw,zl)(z_{w},z_{l}) plane:

  • •

    (i) Entangled increase: both increase, with zwz_{w} faster;

  • •

    (ii) Entangled decrease: both decrease, with zwz_{w} slower;

  • •

    (iii) Disentangled updates: zwz_{w} is not driven downward (and may increase) while zlz_{l} is suppressed.

Pathway (iii) is generally preferable (Yuan et al., 2025) because it suppresses the rejected response while preserving the chosen one, thereby mitigating the likelihood displacement problem (Razin et al., 2025).

However, many margin-based objectives entangle the updates of the chosen and rejected rewards, preventing them from changing independently. This gradient entanglement (Yuan et al., 2025) causes pressure to decrease zlz_{l} often also decreases zwz_{w}, yielding the Pathway (ii) (see Fig. 2(a) for illustration). Such objectives fit the entangled template in Eq. 1, with different settings (see Sec. A.3 for details):

ℒ⁡(zw,zl)=ℓ⁡(hw​(zw)−hl​(zl)−c)+Λ⁡(zw).\mathcal{L}(z_{w},z_{l})=\ell\left(h_{w}(z_{w})-h_{l}(z_{l})-c\right)+\Lambda(z_{w}). (3)

Recently, a growing class of disentangled, density ratio-based objectives (Xiao et al., 2025; Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025) has been observed to often exhibit more disentangled reward dynamics than margin-based objectives, frequently suppressing zlz_{l} without strongly degrading zwz_{w} in many settings (see Fig. 2(a) for a comparison of DPO and DIL-BCE (Xiao et al., 2025)). These objectives are disentangled in the sense that they act on two separate scalars,

ℒ⁡(zw,zl)=ℓw​(zw−zwref)+ℓl​(zl−zlref),\mathcal{L}(z_{w},z_{l})=\ell_{w}(z_{w}-z_{w}^{\text{ref}})+\ell_{l}(z_{l}-z_{l}^{\text{ref}}), (4)

where ℓw\ell_{w} and ℓl\ell_{l} are outer shaping functions corresponding to zwz_{w} and zlz_{l}, respectively. This enables more flexible and potentially asymmetric control over maintaining zwz_{w} versus suppressing zlz_{l}, i.e. Pathway (iii). We summarize this contrast with a schematic comparison in Fig. 2.

However, the underlying mechanism remains unclear. These observations raise a key question: which objective properties determine when training enters the desired Pathway (iii)?

Decomposing the Gradient: Incentives and Scores.

To explain these differences, we look at the gradients. Regardless of whether the objective is entangled (Eq. 3) or disentangled (Eq. 4), the gradient with respect to parameters 𝜽{\bm{\theta}} always decomposes along the same two score directions 𝒔w{\bm{s}}_{w} and 𝒔l{\bm{s}}_{l}. Formally, for any objective ℒ⁡(zw,zl)\mathcal{L}(z_{w},z_{l}), the chain rule yields a unified decomposition of the negative gradient

−∇𝜽ℒ​(zw​(𝜽),zl​(𝜽))\displaystyle-\!\nabla_{\!{\bm{\theta}}}\mathcal{L}(z_{w}({\bm{\theta}}),z_{l}({\bm{\theta}})) =−∂ℒ∂zw​∇𝜽zw​(𝜽)−∂ℒ∂zl​∇𝜽zl​(𝜽)\displaystyle=\!-\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z_{w}}\!\nabla_{\!{\bm{\theta}}}z_{w}({\bm{\theta}})\!-\!\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z_{l}}\!\nabla_{\!{\bm{\theta}}}z_{l}({\bm{\theta}}) (5)
≜dw​(𝜽)​𝒔w​(𝜽)−dl​(𝜽)​𝒔l​(𝜽),\displaystyle\triangleq d_{w}({\bm{\theta}}){\bm{s}}_{w}({\bm{\theta}})\!-\!d_{l}({\bm{\theta}}){\bm{s}}_{l}({\bm{\theta}}),

where dw​(𝜽)≜−∂ℒ∂zw,dl​(𝜽)≜∂ℒ∂zld_{w}({\bm{\theta}})\triangleq-\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z_{w}},d_{l}({\bm{\theta}})\triangleq\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z_{l}} are the incentive coefficients. Eq. 5 reveals a crucial insight: the update directions (𝒔w,𝒔l)({\bm{s}}_{w},{\bm{s}}_{l}) are largely fixed by the model and data (via 𝒔w,𝒔l{\bm{s}}_{w},{\bm{s}}_{l}), while the objective design is entirely distilled into the scalars (dw,dl)(d_{w},d_{l}). These coefficients act as the knobs that control the magnitude and balance of the update. Detailed derivations of (dw,dl)(d_{w},d_{l}) for common objectives are provided in Sec. A.3 and summarized in Tab. 1. In the next subsection, we connect the unified decomposition in Eq. 5 to a continuous-time dynamical system for (zw,zl)(z_{w},z_{l}), which yields an explicit condition for realizing Pathway (iii).

Case Studies: Entangled vs. Disentangled Incentives.

The difference between entangled and disentangled objectives is reflected in their incentive structures (see Tab. 1). Entangled objectives like DPO and IPO have tightly coupled incentives, often symmetric (dw=dld_{w}=d_{l}) or constrained by the shared margin mm, so that increasing the winner inherently affects the loser. Disentangled objectives like DIL-BCE, by contrast, assign independent incentives: dw=σ⁡(−z~w)d_{w}=\sigma(-\tilde{z}_{w}) depends only on the chosen response, while dl=σ⁡(z~l)d_{l}=\sigma(\tilde{z}_{l}) depends only on the rejected one, thereby avoiding the entangled dynamics of margin-based objectives.

3.2 Likelihood Dynamics and Pathway Conditions

By expressing an objective via its incentive coefficients (dw,dl)(d_{w},d_{l}), likelihood analysis reduces to these scalars. Viewing gradient descent as a continuous flow then yields conditions on (dw,dl)(d_{w},d_{l}) for Pathway (iii), revealing structural requirements of the base objective.

Mechanistic Interpretation.

Sec. 3.2 provides a clear mechanistic interpretation of gradient entanglement, revealing that the dynamic of the chosen likelihood, z˙w,t\dot{z}_{w,t}, is governed by two opposing terms. The self-reinforcement term, dw,t​‖𝒔w,t‖2d_{w,t}\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|^{2}, pushes zw,tz_{w,t} upward in proportion to its own incentive and score magnitude. In contrast, the coupling drag term, −dl,t​⟨𝒔w,t,𝒔l,t⟩-d_{l,t}\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\rangle, pulls it downward due to interference from updates targeting the rejected response.

In practice, scores are typically positively correlated (⟨𝒔w,t,𝒔l,t⟩>0\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\rangle>0, as illustrated in Fig. 3(a)). If the objective assigns too much weight to the rejected incentive, e.g., dl,t=dw,td_{l,t}=d_{w,t} as in DPO, the drag can dominate, causing z˙w,t<0\dot{z}_{w,t}<0 even when the desired behavior is to avoid driving zw,tz_{w,t} downward. This explains the squeezing effect (Ren and Sutherland, 2025). These dynamics are local-in-time, so training may enter the desired regime only after an initial transient, consistent with our empirical results (Fig. 2(a)).

Sec. 3.2 shows that margin growth is driven by (dw,t,dl,t)(d_{w,t},d_{l,t}) but regulated by the coupling ⟨𝒔w,t,𝒔l,t⟩\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\rangle, which quantifies winner–loser interaction. We use Sec. 3.2 and Sec. 3.2 as analytical abstractions to expose objective-induced drift and derive sign conditions, rather than to predict exact trajectories.

Conditions of the Three Pathways.

We now translate the qualitative Pathways (i)–(iii) in Sec. 3.1 into local sign conditions implied by the likelihood dynamics in Sec. 3.2. In particular, the Pathway (iii) regime corresponds to z˙w,t≥0\dot{z}_{w,t}\geq 0 and z˙l,t≤0\dot{z}_{l,t}\leq 0.

The key observation is that these signs depend on how strongly the objective updates the winner versus the loser relative to their score coupling. We therefore normalize the coupling term via the cosine similarity:

ρt≜⟨𝒔w,t,𝒔l,t⟩‖𝒔w,t‖​‖𝒔l,t‖∈[−1,1].\rho_{t}\triangleq\frac{\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\rangle}{\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|}\in[-1,1]. (7)

We focus on the challenging regime where ρt>0\rho_{t}>0, which is typical in fine-tuning tasks (see Fig. 3(a)). For standard preference objectives, we typically have dw,t>0d_{w,t}>0 and dl,t>0d_{l,t}>0 (see Tab. 1). Substituting ⟨𝒔w,t,𝒔l,t⟩=ρt​‖𝒔w,t‖​‖𝒔l,t‖\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\rangle=\rho_{t}\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\| into Eq. 6 in Sec. 3.2 and factoring out dl,td_{l,t} yields

z˙w,t\displaystyle\dot{z}_{w,t} =dl,t​‖𝒔w,t‖2​(dw,tdl,t−ρt​‖𝒔l,t‖‖𝒔w,t‖),\displaystyle=d_{l,t}\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|^{2}\left(\frac{d_{w,t}}{d_{l,t}}-\rho_{t}\frac{\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|}{\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|}\right), (8)
z˙l,t\displaystyle\dot{z}_{l,t} =dl,t​‖𝒔l,t‖2​(ρt​‖𝒔w,t‖‖𝒔l,t‖​dw,tdl,t−1).\displaystyle=d_{l,t}\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|^{2}\left(\rho_{t}\frac{\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|}{\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|}\frac{d_{w,t}}{d_{l,t}}-1\right).

Hence the signs of (z˙w,t,z˙l,t)(\dot{z}_{w,t},\dot{z}_{l,t}) are governed by where the ratio dw,t/dl,td_{w,t}/d_{l,t} falls relative to two thresholds, ρt​‖𝒔l,t‖‖𝒔w,t‖\rho_{t}\tfrac{\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|}{\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|} and 1ρt​‖𝒔l,t‖‖𝒔w,t‖\tfrac{1}{\rho_{t}}\tfrac{\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|}{\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|}, which partition the ratio axis into three regimes that exactly match Pathways (i)-(iii), as summaried in Tab. 2.

Disentanglement Band.

Only the second regime in Tab. 2 permits the Pathway (iii). Equivalently, the conditions of Pathway (iii), i.e., (z˙w,t,z˙l,t)=(≥0,≤0)\left(\dot{z}_{w,t},\dot{z}_{l,t}\right)=(\geq 0,\leq 0) hold if

log⁡‖𝒔l,t‖‖𝒔w,t‖+log⁡ρt≤log⁡rt≤log⁡‖𝒔l,t‖‖𝒔w,t‖−log⁡ρt,\log\frac{\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|}{\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|}+\log\rho_{t}\leq\log r_{t}\leq\log\frac{\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|}{\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|}-\log\rho_{t}, (9)

where rt≜dw,t/dl,tr_{t}\triangleq d_{w,t}/d_{l,t} for simplicity. We term this interval the disentanglement band (DB), since any log⁡rt\log r_{t} within this band makes the sign pattern (z˙w,t,z˙l,t)=(≥0,≤0)(\dot{z}_{w,t},\dot{z}_{l,t})=(\geq 0,\leq 0) feasible under Eq. 8, i.e., it admits Pathway (iii) at time tt.

Interpreting the Band.

The DB provides a unified explanation for the behavior of different objectives (Tab. 2):

  • •

    Inside DB: The incentive ratio rtr_{t} is balanced to overcome the correlation ρt\rho_{t}. The update suppresses the loser without driving the winner downward (Pathway (iii)).

  • •

    Below DB (rt<ρt​‖𝒔l,t‖‖𝒔w,t‖r_{t}<\rho_{t}\tfrac{\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|}{\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|}): The chosen incentive dw,td_{w,t} is too weak relative to dl,td_{l,t}. The “drag” from the loser update pulls zwz_{w} down (Pathway (ii)).

  • •

    Above DB (rt>1ρt​‖𝒔l,t‖‖𝒔w,t‖r_{t}>\frac{1}{\rho_{t}}\frac{\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|}{\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|}): The chosen incentive is too strong, causing both zwz_{w} and zlz_{l} to rise (Pathway (i)).

Crucially, the DB width is 2​|log⁡ρt|2|\log\rho_{t}|. As ρt→1\rho_{t}\to 1, the band collapses, leaving little room to satisfy (z˙w,t,z˙l,t)=(≥0,≤0)(\dot{z}_{w,t},\dot{z}_{l,t})=(\geq 0,\leq 0) under first-order analysis. Yet ρt<1\rho_{t}<1 in practice, yielding a feasible optimization window (Fig. 3(a)).

When Disentanglement Succeeds?

Two factors determine disentanglement success: (1) ρt\rho_{t} sets the feasible DB width in Eq. 9, and (2) the objective determines where the realized log-ratio log⁡rt\log r_{t} lands within DB.

Thus, a wide DB alone is insufficient: entanglement persists if log⁡rt\log r_{t} consistently lies outside the band or clusters near its thresholds. This behavior is evident in Fig. 3. For instance, CPO achieves small ρt\rho_{t} (hence a wide DB) but often pushes rtr_{t} to the upper edge or beyond (Fig. 3(c)), following Pathway (i) (Fig. 3(b)). In contrast, disentangled objectives like DIL-BCE keep rtr_{t} stably inside the DB and closer to its center (Fig. 3(d)), aligning with Pathway (iii).

Moreover, from Eq. 8, the lower edge of the DB corresponds exactly to the locus where z˙w,t=0\dot{z}_{w,t}=0. Slightly above this edge, the winner remains nearly stable while z˙l,t<0\dot{z}_{l,t}<0 is still enforced. In practice, however, rtr_{t} is not a deterministic knob: it fluctuates over steps and across triplets under mini-batch sampling and adaptive optimization. Consequently, a robust objective should keep rtr_{t} stably inside DB rather than merely avoiding crossing the lower edge. This motivates analyzing where log⁡rt\log r_{t} sits within DB, beyond feasibility.

Where the Log-Ratio Should Sit?

To maximize robustness against multiplicative fluctuations in the ratio, we seek the point that maximizes the log-distance to the nearest threshold. Let Δt​(log⁡rt)\Delta_{t}(\log r_{t}) denote the minimum distance from log⁡rt\log r_{t} to the lower and upper thresholds of the DB:

Δt​(log⁡rt)≜min⁡(log⁡rt​‖𝒔w,t‖ρt​‖𝒔l,t‖,log⁡‖𝒔l,t‖ρt​rt​‖𝒔w,t‖).\!\Delta_{t}(\log r_{t})\!\triangleq\!\min\left(\log\frac{r_{t}\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|}{\rho_{t}\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|},\log\frac{\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|}{\rho_{t}r_{t}\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|}\right). (10)

Then Δt​(log⁡rt)≥0\Delta_{t}(\log r_{t})\geq 0 if and only if rtr_{t} lies inside DB, and larger Δt​(log⁡rt)\Delta_{t}(\log r_{t}) means more tolerance to multiplicative fluctuations of log⁡rt\log r_{t} while preserving pathway (iii).

Proposition \thetheorem.

For given ρt\rho_{t} and ‖𝐬l,t‖/‖𝐬w,t‖\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|/\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|, the maximizer of Δt​(log⁡rt)\Delta_{t}(\log r_{t}) over all log⁡rt\log r_{t} inside DB satisfies

log⁡rt⋆=arg⁡maxlog⁡rt∈DB​Δt​(log⁡rt)=log⁡‖𝒔l,t‖‖𝒔w,t‖.\log r_{t}^{\star}=\arg\max_{\log r_{t}\in\text{DB}}\Delta_{t}(\log r_{t})=\log\frac{\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|}{\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|}. (11)

See Sec. B.3 for a detailed proof. The robust center log⁡rt⋆\log r_{t}^{\star} balances the score vector norms. To maintain stability, incentives should be inversely proportional to the gradient magnitudes of the respective likelihoods.

3.3 Plug-and-Play Reward Calibration

A natural next question is: how can we make the realized log-ratio log⁡rt\log r_{t} track log⁡rt⋆\log r_{t}^{\star} during stochastic training?

Based on this robust centering, we propose a simple wrapper method: reward calibration (RC). Instead of redesigning the objective function ℒ\mathcal{L} from scratch, we can adaptively rescale the likelihood gradients to make log⁡rt\log r_{t} track log⁡rt⋆\log r_{t}^{\star}.

We define the calibrated likelihoods as follows:

zw,trc≜(rt⋆rt)1/2​zw,t+(1−(rt⋆rt)1/2)​sg⁡(zw,t),\displaystyle z_{w,t}^{\rm rc}\triangleq\Bigl(\frac{r_{t}^{\star}}{r_{t}}\Bigr)^{1/2}z_{w,t}+\Bigl(1-\Bigl(\frac{r_{t}^{\star}}{r_{t}}\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigr)\operatorname{sg}(z_{w,t}), (12)
zl,trc≜(rt⋆rt)−1/2zl,t+(1−(rt⋆rt)−1/2)sg(zl,t),\displaystyle z_{l,t}^{\rm rc}\triangleq\Bigl(\frac{r_{t}^{\star}}{r_{t}}\Bigr)^{-1/2}z_{l,t}+\Bigl(1-\Bigl(\frac{r_{t}^{\star}}{r_{t}}\Bigr)^{-1/2}\Bigr)\operatorname{sg}(z_{l,t}),

where sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}(\cdot) denotes a stop-gradient operator, satisfying sg⁡(x)=x\operatorname{sg}(x)=x and ∂∂x​sg⁡(x)=0\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\operatorname{sg}(x)=0.

Applying the base objective ℒ\mathcal{L} to the calibrated likelihoods leaves the forward pass unchanged (zrc=zz^{\rm rc}=z), but scales the backward gradients by (rt⋆/rt)1/2(r_{t}^{\star}/r_{t})^{1/2} and (rt⋆/rt)−1/2(r_{t}^{\star}/r_{t})^{-1/2}, respectively. This adaptively calibrates the incentive coefficients (dw,t,dl,t)(d_{w,t},d_{l,t}) so that the incentive log-ratio aligns with the target center log⁡rt⋆\log r_{t}^{\star}, rectifying the dynamics on the fly. The next proposition formalizes this effect.

Proposition \thetheorem.

The log-ratio induced by the calibrated likelihoods in Eq. 12 is exactly the log-ratio log⁡rt⋆\log r_{t}^{\star} defined in Sec. 3.2.

See Sec. B.4 for a detailed proof.

Building on Sec. 3.3, we introduce a plug-and-play calibration wrapper applicable to a broad class of preference optimization methods. The procedure is summarized in Algorithm 1, with a PyTorch implementation provided in Algorithm 2. Importantly, the method requires no changes to the underlying optimizer and objective formulations; it merely rescales likelihood gradients via calibrated inputs (zw,trc,zl,trc)(z_{w,t}^{\rm rc},z_{l,t}^{\rm rc}) to promote the Pathway (iii) regime by keeping the incentive ratio in (and near the center of) the DB.

Practical Implementations for Reward Calibration.

To ensure efficiency and numerical stability, we adopt two implementation choices. First, we approximate the scores (‖𝒔w,t‖,‖𝒔l,t‖)(\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|,\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|) using gradients from the output layer: the language model head in full fine-tuning, or the final adapter modules in LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) or QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023). Empirically, this avoids the cost of a full backward pass and yields similar DB values to full-parameter gradients (see Fig. 6 in Sec. C.3). Second, to reduce the high variance of stochastic gradients with batch size 11, we use log-domain exponential moving averages (EMA) to estimate the geometric mean of log⁡rt⋆\log r_{t}^{\star} and log⁡rt\log r_{t} for calibration. Further details are in Sec. C.3.

4 Experimental Verifications

4.1 Experimental Settings

Model and Benchmarks.

All models are trained for 11 epoch using AdamW with a constant learning rate (no warm-up) and a global batch size of 3232. The learning rates are set per model scale and are consistent across baselines: Pythia-410M: 6​e−76e-7, Pythia-2.8B: 1​e−41e-4, Mistral-7B: 3​e−73e-7, Qwen2.5-7B: 5​e−75e-7. Experiments were run on two NVIDIA RTX 5090 D and six NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs.

We evaluate our RC method using the UltraFeedback Binarized dataset (Cui et al., 2024; Tunstall et al., 2024) and Anthropic Helpful and Harmless‌ (Antropic-HH) (Bai et al., 2022). Our experiments employ Pythia-410M, Pythia-2.8B (Biderman et al., 2023), Mistral-7B-Base (Tunstall et al., 2024), and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024) as the backbone architectures.

To assess robustness across different training regimes, we apply full-parameter fine-tuning on Pythia-410M and use QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) for the other larger models. This setup ensures that our calibration method works across both full-weight updates and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

We evaluate methods on the Open LLM Leaderboard (Gao et al., 2024), focusing on open-ended conversational alignment using AlpacaEval 2.0 (Dubois et al., 2024) with DeepSeek V3.2 (Liu et al., 2025), reporting the Length-Controlled Win Rate (LC Win Rate).

Baselines and Implementation.

We compare our framework against two categories of baselines:

(1) Entangled objectives: margin-based methods that entangle the updates of chosen and rejected responses, such as DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023), IPO (Azar et al., 2024), and their variants CPO (Xu et al., 2024a), SimPO (Meng et al., 2024) and TI-DPO (Yang et al., 2026).

(2) Disentangled objectives: density ratio estimation methods that offer more independent control over updates, including DDRO (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025) and the DIL family (BCE, LSIF, UKL) (Xiao et al., 2025).

4.2 Ablation Studies

We next examine two practical design choices in RC: approximating the score norms using output-side gradients, and stabilizing the ratio estimates with log-domain EMA.

Efficient DB Estimation.

Computing the exact score norms ‖𝒔w,t‖,‖𝒔l,t‖\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|,\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\| requires a full backward pass through all trainable parameters. To make RC practical, we approximate them using output-side parameters: the language modeling head in full fine-tuning, and the final trainable adapter layers in parameter-efficient fine-tuning (e.g., LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) or QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023)). On Mistral-7B, the resulting DB closely matches the full-parameter version in both width and trend (Fig. 5), supporting this efficient approximation.

Sensitivity to EMA Momentum.

RC uses log-domain EMA to stabilize ratio estimates during stochastic training. We ablate the EMA momentum on Pythia-2.8B with DPO using β∈{0.5,0.9,0.95,0.98,0.999}\beta\in\{0.5,0.9,0.95,0.98,0.999\}. As shown in Tab. 3, performance is very similar across this range, indicating that RC is not sensitive to the EMA momentum and remains effective over a broad range of smoothing strengths.

Training-Time Overhead of Reward Calibration.

RC is a lightweight backward-pass wrapper that introduces no auxiliary model or extra forward pass. Its wall-clock overhead is negligible under LoRA fine-tuning (Mistral-7B: ∼\sim11h →\rightarrow ∼\sim11.4h; Pythia-2.8B: ∼\sim4.5h with little observed delay) and modest under full-parameter tuning on Pythia-410M (∼\sim50m →\rightarrow ∼\sim59m). Detailed timings are reported in Tab. 8.

4.3 Experimental Results for Reward Calibration

Verifying Pathway (iii) via Reward Calibration.

RC is designed to enforce Pathway (iii) by keeping the realized log-ratio log⁡rt\log r_{t} inside the DB and near the center log⁡rt⋆\log r_{t}^{\star}. On Pythia-2.8B (Fig. 4), entangled baselines align with the DB-based diagnosis: DPO/IPO frequently exhibit winner degradation together with loser suppression (Pathway (ii)), while CPO can instead drift toward joint increase (Pathway (i)). Importantly, objective form alone does not guarantee Pathway (iii): DDRO on Pythia-2.8B can also deviate from the DB-feasible regime and correspondingly fail to realize Pathway (iii) (see Fig. 10(a) in Sec. C.5). After applying RC, trajectories more often enter and remain in the Pathway (iii) regime across objectives and model scales from Pythia-410M to Mistral-7B (see Figs. 8(d), 9(e), 10(d), 11(d) and 12(c) for the full results).

Downstream Performance Comparison On Benchmarks.

Tabs. 4 and 9 compares downstream performance with (w/) and without (w/o) RC. Overall, RC is more helpful when the uncalibrated run exhibits entangled or unstable likelihood dynamics, as rebalancing chosen vs. rejected updates facilitates training toward Pathway (iii).

On Pythia-2.8B, the clearest gains appear on ARC and BBH. For example, DPO improves ARC from 34.0434.04 to 37.1237.12 (+3.08+3.08), SimPO improves ARC from 32.5932.59 to 37.0337.03 (+4.44+4.44) and BBH from 30.4930.49 to 31.3431.34 (+0.85+0.85), and TI-DPO improves the average score from 27.1327.13 to 28.4428.44 (+1.31+1.31). In contrast, the effect is more task-dependent on MMLU-PRO and MUSR, where we observe both gains and regressions (e.g., MMLU-PRO improves for DPO/BCE/SimPO/TI-DPO but drops for CPO), consistent with RC being a dynamics-oriented intervention rather than a guaranteed monotonic booster.

On Mistral-7B, RC mainly acts as a stabilizer for weak runs. DPO improves from 24.2624.26 to 36.4436.44 on average (+12.18+12.18), with MMLU-Pro increasing from 11.6611.66 to 30.3130.31 and ARC from 22.7022.70 to 60.9260.92. DDRO shows a similar recovery, improving from 16.5316.53 to 36.3436.34 on average (+19.81+19.81). When the baseline is already strong, the changes are small, e.g., SimPO (+0.01+0.01), BCE (−0.05-0.05), LSIF (+0.15+0.15), and TI-DPO (+0.00+0.00) in average score. When the baseline is already strong (e.g., BCE/SimPO/LSIF), RC is non-disruptive, with changes typically near zero.

On Qwen2.5-7B, remains non-disruptive and brings modest improvements for most objectives. The average score improves for DPO (+0.48+0.48), SimPO (+0.26+0.26), BCE (+1.33+1.33), LSIF (+0.23+0.23), and TI-DPO (+0.11+0.11), while CPO is nearly unchanged (+0.01+0.01) and DDRO shows a small drop (−0.05-0.05). The gains are smaller than those on Mistral-7B, but the overall trend is still consistent with our main claim: promoting the Pathway (iii) regime is a useful and generally safe intervention, with clear gains in many entangled/unstable settings. See Sec. C.4 for detailed analysis.

Downstream Performance Comparison On Open-Ended Generation.

To assess open-ended generation, we further evaluate RC-calibrated Pythia-2.8B models against baselines on AlpacaEval 2.0 judged by DeepSeek V3.2 (Liu et al., 2025). RC improves the entangled DPO variant to a 70.56% win rate (similar to 70.12% via GPT-4-Turbo11 1 https://openai.com/api/), while remaining non-regressive for the already-disentangled BCE variant (51.4351.43%). This suggests that RC is particularly helpful for entangled objectives, while remaining non-regressive for the disentangled BCE variant in Pathway (iii) in this experiment.

5 Conclusion and Future Works

Conclusion.

We presented a unified framework for diagnosing and mitigating likelihood displacement in preference optimization. Through an incentive-score decomposition, we showed that diverse objectives share identical update directions and differ only in scalar incentive coefficients. This led to the disentanglement band (DB), a testable condition that characterizes when training avoids likelihood displacement by entering the Pathway (iii) regime (chosen not down, rejected not up, possibly after an initial transient). To enforce this condition, we introduced reward calibration (RC), a plug-and-play wrapper that rebalances chosen vs. rejected updates without redesigning the base objective. Empirically, RC often steers training toward Pathway (iii) and improves downstream alignment across diverse objectives and model scales.

Limitations and Future Work.

Future work includes exploring other objective-agnostic ways to encourage Pathway (iii), extending the framework to iterative or online preference optimization, and generalizing the current pairwise setting to multi-response preference data.

Appendix

Appendix A Notations and Preliminaries

A.1 Notations

In this section, we summarize all the symbols used in this paper. See Tab. 6 for details.

A.2 Supplementary Related Works

Density Ratio Estimation.

Density ratio estimation (DRE) is a classical statistical problem in machine learning (Sugiyama et al., 2012). Early discriminative/contrastive estimators include KLIEP (Sugiyama et al., 2008) and NCE (Gutmann and Hyvärinen, 2010; Gutmann and Hyvärinen, 2012), but they can be unstable under limited support overlap (Liu et al., 2017). More recent score-based DRE introduces intermediate distributions, ranging from discrete TRE (Rhodes et al., 2020) to continuous path formulations such as DRE-∞\infty (Choi et al., 2021), with refinements via diffusion-bridge interpolants (Chen et al., 2025b), adaptive iterative paths based on the minimum variance path principle (Chen et al., 2026a), conditional probability path (Yu et al., 2025), and one-step score-based estimators (Chen et al., 2026b). The broader field of probabilistic inference (Paisley and Carin, 2009; Xu and Zeng, 2024) and Gaussian processes (Xu et al., 2024c; Xu et al., 2024b), robust logical and semantic capabilities (Zhang et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026; Bao et al., 2025) and generative modeling (Chen et al., 2025a; Xu et al., 2025) has also advanced sampling and inference techniques that underpin several of these estimators for capturing complex data structures (Li et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025b; Lin et al., 2025). This literature provides context for density ratio-motivated preference objectives (e.g., DIL (Xiao et al., 2025), DDRO (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025)). In contrast, we do not design new DRE estimators but analyze when such shaping yields disentangled likelihood dynamics and propose a plug-and-play intervention.

A.3 Incentive Coefficients for Entangled and Disentangled Objectives

In this appendix we derive the incentive coefficients (dw,dl)(d_{w},d_{l}) that appear in the unified update

−∇𝜽ℒ​(zw​(𝜽),zl​(𝜽))=−∂ℒ∂zw​∇𝜽zw​(𝜽)−∂ℒ∂zl​∇𝜽zl​(𝜽)≜dw​(𝜽)​𝒔w​(𝜽)−dl​(𝜽)​𝒔l​(𝜽).\displaystyle-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(z_{w}({\bm{\theta}}),z_{l}({\bm{\theta}}))=-\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z_{w}}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}z_{w}({\bm{\theta}})-\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z_{l}}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}z_{l}({\bm{\theta}})\triangleq d_{w}({\bm{\theta}}){\bm{s}}_{w}({\bm{\theta}})-d_{l}({\bm{\theta}}){\bm{s}}_{l}({\bm{\theta}}). (13)

We define incentive coefficients as

dw≜−∂ℒ∂zw,dl≜∂ℒ∂zl.d_{w}\triangleq-\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z_{w}},\qquad d_{l}\triangleq\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z_{l}}. (14)

For derivations, it is convenient to distinguish objectives by whether they are entangled (the loss ties zwz_{w} and zlz_{l} through a shared scalar, coupling dwd_{w} and dld_{l}) or disentangled (separate shaping of chosen vs. rejected terms, allowing more independent dwd_{w} and dld_{l}). This structural distinction on (dw,dl)(d_{w},d_{l}) should not be conflated with density ratio-based vs. margin-based design (e.g., DIL (Xiao et al., 2025) vs. KTO (Ethayarajh et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2025)). When a reference policy πref\pi_{\text{ref}} is used, zwref,zlrefz_{w}^{\text{ref}},z_{l}^{\text{ref}} are treated as constants.

A.3.1 Entangled Objectives

We consider entangled objectives of the form (Yuan et al., 2025)

ℒ⁡(zw,zl)=ℓ⁡(hw​(zw)−hl​(zl)−c)+Λ⁡(zw),\mathcal{L}(z_{w},z_{l})=\ell\left(h_{w}(z_{w})-h_{l}(z_{l})-c\right)+\Lambda(z_{w}), (15)

where ℓ⁡(⋅)\ell(\cdot) is an outer shaping function, hw,hlh_{w},h_{l} are transformations, cc is a constant offset (e.g., induced by a reference policy or length correction), and Λ⁡(zw)\Lambda(z_{w}) is an optional chosen-only term (e.g., a likelihood regularizer in SlicHF (Zhao et al., 2023)). Substituting Eq. 15 into the definitions in Eq. 14 and applying the chain rule, we obtain

dw\displaystyle d_{w} =−ℓ′​(hw​(zw)−hl​(zl)−c)​hw′​(zw)−Λ′​(zw),\displaystyle=-\ell^{\prime}\left(h_{w}(z_{w})-h_{l}(z_{l})-c\right)h_{w}^{\prime}(z_{w})-\Lambda^{\prime}(z_{w}), (16)
dl\displaystyle d_{l} =ℓ′​(hw​(zw)−hl​(zl)−c)​hl′​(zl),\displaystyle=\ell^{\prime}\left(h_{w}(z_{w})-h_{l}(z_{l})-c\right)h_{l}^{\prime}(z_{l}),

where ℓ′\ell^{\prime} denotes the derivative of ℓ\ell with respect to its scalar argument, and hw′h_{w}^{\prime}, hl′h_{l}^{\prime}, and Λ′\Lambda^{\prime} denote the derivatives of hwh_{w}, hlh_{l}, and Λ\Lambda with respect to their respective inputs (zwz_{w} or zlz_{l}). This notation is used throughout this subsection.

Below we instantiate Eq. 16 for common objectives.

DPO.

DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) uses ℒDPO​(zw,zl)=−log⁡σ⁡(β⁡((zw−zl)−(zwref−zlref)))\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}(z_{w},z_{l})=-\log\sigma\left(\beta\left((z_{w}-z_{l})-(z_{w}^{\text{ref}}-z_{l}^{\text{ref}})\right)\right). This corresponds to hw​(zw)=β​zwh_{w}(z_{w})=\beta z_{w}, hl​(zl)=β​zlh_{l}(z_{l})=\beta z_{l}, c=β⁡(zwref−zlref)c=\beta(z_{w}^{\text{ref}}-z_{l}^{\text{ref}}), and Λ⁡(zw)≡0\Lambda(z_{w})\equiv 0. Since dd​u​[−log⁡σ⁡(u)]=−σ⁡(−u)\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}u}\left[-\log\sigma(u)\right]=-\sigma(-u), we obtain

dw=dl=β​σ​(−β​m~),d_{w}=d_{l}=\beta\sigma\left(-\beta\tilde{m}\right), (17)

where m~=(zw−zl)−(zwref−zlref)\tilde{m}=(z_{w}-z_{l})-(z_{w}^{\text{ref}}-z_{l}^{\text{ref}}).

IPO.

IPO (Azar et al., 2024, identity preference optimization) uses ℒIPO​(zw,zl)=(m~−λ)2\mathcal{L}_{\text{IPO}}(z_{w},z_{l})=(\tilde{m}-\lambda)^{2}. Here hw​(zw)=zwh_{w}(z_{w})=z_{w}, hl​(zl)=zlh_{l}(z_{l})=z_{l}, c=zwref−zlrefc=z_{w}^{\text{ref}}-z_{l}^{\text{ref}}, Λ⁡(zw)≡0\Lambda(z_{w})\equiv 0, and ℓ⁡(u)=(u−λ)2\ell(u)=(u-\lambda)^{2}, hence ℓ′​(u)=2​(u−λ)\ell^{\prime}(u)=2(u-\lambda). Therefore, we have

dw=dl=2​(λ−m~).d_{w}=d_{l}=2(\lambda-\tilde{m}). (18)
R-DPO.

R-DPO (Park et al., 2024, regularized-DPO) modifies the DPO argument by a length-difference correction: ℒR-DPO​(zw,zl)=−log⁡σ⁡(β​m~+α​Δ​|𝒚|)\mathcal{L}_{\text{R-DPO}}(z_{w},z_{l})=-\log\sigma(\beta\tilde{m}+\alpha\Delta|{\bm{y}}|), where Δ​|𝒚|=|𝒚w|−|𝒚l|\Delta|{\bm{y}}|=|{\bm{y}}_{w}|-|{\bm{y}}_{l}|. Here, hw​(zw)=β​zwh_{w}(z_{w})=\beta z_{w}, hl​(zl)=β​zlh_{l}(z_{l})=\beta z_{l}, Λ⁡(zw)≡0\Lambda(z_{w})\equiv 0, and a modified offset c=β⁡(zwref−zlref)−α​Δ​|𝒚|c=\beta(z_{w}^{\text{ref}}-z_{l}^{\text{ref}})-\alpha\Delta|{\bm{y}}|. The resulting incentive coefficients are

dw=dl=β​σ​(−β​m~−α​Δ​|𝒚|).d_{w}=d_{l}=\beta\sigma\left(-\beta\tilde{m}-\alpha\Delta|{\bm{y}}|\right). (19)
SimPO.

SimPO (Meng et al., 2024, simple preference optimization) uses a length-normalized margin mnorm=β|𝒚w|​zw−β|𝒚l|​zlm_{\text{norm}}\!=\!\frac{\beta}{|{\bm{y}}_{w}|}z_{w}\!-\!\frac{\beta}{|{\bm{y}}_{l}|}z_{l} and loss ℒSimPO​(zw,zl)=−log⁡σ⁡(mnorm−γ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{SimPO}}(z_{w},z_{l})\!=\!-\log\sigma(m_{\text{norm}}-\gamma). With hw​(zw)=β|𝒚w|​zwh_{w}(z_{w})\!=\!\frac{\beta}{|{\bm{y}}_{w}|}z_{w}, hl​(zl)=β|𝒚l|​zlh_{l}(z_{l})\!=\!\frac{\beta}{|{\bm{y}}_{l}|}z_{l}, c=γc\!=\!\gamma, and Λ⁡(zw)≡0\Lambda(z_{w})\!\equiv\!0, we get

dw=β|𝒚w|​σ​(γ−mnorm),dl=β|𝒚l|​σ​(γ−mnorm).d_{w}=\frac{\beta}{|{\bm{y}}_{w}|}\sigma(\gamma-m_{\text{norm}}),\qquad d_{l}=\frac{\beta}{|{\bm{y}}_{l}|}\sigma(\gamma-m_{\text{norm}}). (20)
CPO.

CPO (Xu et al., 2024a, contrastive preference optimization) augments the standard margin loss with a chosen-only likelihood term: ℒCPO​(zw,zl)=−log⁡σ⁡(β​m)−λ​zw\mathcal{L}_{\text{CPO}}(z_{w},z_{l})=-\log\sigma(\beta m)-\lambda z_{w}, where m=zw−zlm=z_{w}-z_{l}. This corresponds to hw​(zw)=β​zwh_{w}(z_{w})=\beta z_{w}, hl​(zl)=β​zlh_{l}(z_{l})=\beta z_{l}, and c=0c=0. Crucially, it sets Λ⁡(zw)=−λ​zw\Lambda(z_{w})=-\lambda z_{w}, so that minimizing ℒCPO\mathcal{L}_{\text{CPO}} encourages larger zwz_{w}. Therefore

dw=β​σ​(−β​m)+λ,dl=β​σ​(−β​m).d_{w}=\beta\sigma(-\beta m)+\lambda,\qquad d_{l}=\beta\sigma(-\beta m). (21)
RRHF / SlicHF.

Hinge-style objectives such as RRHF (Yuan et al., 2023) and SlicHF (Zhao et al., 2023) use

ℒhinge​(zw,zl)=max⁡(0,γ−m)−λ​zw,m=zw−zl,\mathcal{L}_{\text{hinge}}(z_{w},z_{l})=\max(0,\gamma-m)-\lambda z_{w},\qquad m=z_{w}-z_{l}, (22)

where γ=0\gamma=0 recovers RRHF. Here hw​(zw)=zwh_{w}(z_{w})=z_{w}, hl​(zl)=zlh_{l}(z_{l})=z_{l}, c=0c=0, and Λ⁡(zw)=−λ​zw\Lambda(z_{w})=-\lambda z_{w}. Using a subgradient for the hinge term, ∂∂m​max⁡(0,γ−m)=−𝕀⁡(m<γ)\frac{\partial}{\partial m}\max(0,\gamma-m)=-\mathbb{I}(m<\gamma), we obtain

dl=𝕀⁡(m<γ),dw=𝕀⁡(m<γ)+λ.d_{l}=\mathbb{I}(m<\gamma),\qquad d_{w}=\mathbb{I}(m<\gamma)+\lambda. (23)
TDPO.

For TDPO (Zeng et al., 2024, token-level DPO), we keep the winner-side statistic unchanged and absorb the rejected-side token-level correction into the loser-side statistic: zl≜logπ𝜽(𝒚l∣𝒙)+αDSeqKL(𝒙,𝒚l;πref∥π𝜽)z_{l}\triangleq\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}({\bm{y}}_{l}\mid{\bm{x}})+\alpha D_{\mathrm{SeqKL}}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{l};\pi_{\text{ref}}\|\pi_{\bm{\theta}}), where

DSeqKL(𝒙,𝒚;πref∥πθ)=∑t=1|𝒚|DKL(πref(⋅∣[𝒙,𝒚<t])∥πθ(⋅∣[𝒙,𝒚<t])).D_{\mathrm{SeqKL}}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}};\pi_{\text{ref}}\|\pi_{\theta})=\sum_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}|}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid[{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{<t}])\middle\|\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid[{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{<t}])\right). (24)

Define Dw≜DSeqKL(𝒙,𝒚w;πref∥π𝜽)D_{w}\triangleq D_{\mathrm{SeqKL}}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{w};\pi_{\text{ref}}\|\pi_{\bm{\theta}}), then TDPO can be written as ℒTDPO​(zw,zl)=−log⁡σ⁡(β⁡[m~+α​sg⁡(Dw)])\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TDPO}}(z_{w},z_{l})=-\log\sigma(\beta[\tilde{m}+\alpha\operatorname{sg}(D_{w})]). Therefore,

dw=−∂ℒTDPO∂zw=β​σ​(−β⁡[m~+α​sg⁡(Dw)]),dl=∂ℒTDPO∂zl=β​σ​(−β⁡[m~+α​sg⁡(Dw)]).d_{w}=-\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TDPO}}}{\partial z_{w}}=\beta\sigma(-\beta[\tilde{m}+\alpha\operatorname{sg}(D_{w})]),\qquad d_{l}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TDPO}}}{\partial z_{l}}=\beta\sigma(-\beta[\tilde{m}+\alpha\operatorname{sg}(D_{w})]). (25)

The corresponding scores are 𝒔w=∇𝜽​log​π𝜽​(𝒚w∣𝒙){\bm{s}}_{w}=\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}({\bm{y}}_{w}\mid{\bm{x}}) and 𝒔l=∇𝜽logπ𝜽(𝒚l∣𝒙)+α∇𝜽DSeqKL(𝒙,𝒚l;πref∥π𝜽){\bm{s}}_{l}=\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}({\bm{y}}_{l}\mid{\bm{x}})+\alpha\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}D_{\mathrm{SeqKL}}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{l};\pi_{\text{ref}}\|\pi_{\bm{\theta}}). Hence TDPO still admits the same two-branch decomposition −∇𝜽ℒTDPO=dw​𝒔w−dl​𝒔l-\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TDPO}}=d_{w}{\bm{s}}_{w}-d_{l}{\bm{s}}_{l}. Therefore, TDPO remains entangled: it preserves the symmetric incentive coefficients dw=dld_{w}=d_{l}, while modifying the loser-side score direction through an additional token-level sequential KL term.

TI-DPO.

For the weighted token-level preference term in TI-DPO (Yang et al., 2026, token-importance DPO), define the winner/loser branch statistics as weighted sums of token-level log-probabilities:

zw≜∑t=1|𝒚w|ωw,t​log⁡π𝜽​(yw,t∣[𝒙,𝒚w,<t]),zl≜∑t=1|𝒚l|ωl,t​log⁡π𝜽​(yl,t∣[𝒙,𝒚l,<t]),z_{w}\triangleq\sum_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}_{w}|}\omega_{w,t}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(y_{w,t}\mid[{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{w,<t}]),\qquad z_{l}\triangleq\sum_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}_{l}|}\omega_{l,t}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(y_{l,t}\mid[{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{l,<t}]), (26)

where ωw,t\omega_{w,t} and ωl,t\omega_{l,t} are the token-importance weights. Define zwrefz_{w}^{\text{ref}} and zlrefz_{l}^{\text{ref}} analogously by replacing π𝜽\pi_{\bm{\theta}} with πref\pi_{\text{ref}}. Then the weighted DPO term in TI-DPO takes the standard entangled form ℒTI​-​DPO=−log⁡σ⁡(β​m~)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TI\text{-}DPO}}=-\log\sigma(\beta\tilde{m}). Its incentive coefficients are therefore

dw=β​σ​(−β​m~),dl=β​σ​(−β​m~).d_{w}=\beta\sigma(-\beta\tilde{m}),\qquad d_{l}=\beta\sigma(-\beta\tilde{m}). (27)

The corresponding score directions become token-weighted sums:

𝒔w=∑t=1|𝒚w|ωw,t​∇𝜽​log⁡π𝜽​(yw,t∣[𝒙,𝒚w,<t]),𝒔l=∑t=1|𝒚l|ωl,t​∇𝜽​log⁡π𝜽​(yl,t∣[𝒙,𝒚l,<t]).{\bm{s}}_{w}=\sum_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}_{w}|}\omega_{w,t}\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(y_{w,t}\mid[{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{w,<t}]),\qquad{\bm{s}}_{l}=\sum_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}_{l}|}\omega_{l,t}\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(y_{l,t}\mid[{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{l,<t}]). (28)

Therefore, the token-level weighting changes the branch statistics and the resulting score directions, but not the form of the incentive coefficients.

A.3.2 Disentangled Objectives

Disentangled objectives decompose into independent chosen and rejected terms, typically through reference-normalized log density ratios z~w≜zw−zwref\tilde{z}_{w}\triangleq z_{w}-z_{w}^{\text{ref}} and z~l≜zl−zlref\tilde{z}_{l}\triangleq z_{l}-z_{l}^{\text{ref}}. In entangled objectives, there is only one outer shaping function ℓ\ell, while a general disentangled form is

ℒ⁡(zw,zl)=ℓw​(z~w)+ℓl​(z~l),\mathcal{L}(z_{w},z_{l})=\ell_{w}(\tilde{z}_{w})+\ell_{l}(\tilde{z}_{l}), (29)

for which

dw=−ℓw′​(z~w)=−∂∂z~w​ℓw​(z~w),dl=ℓl′​(z~l)=∂∂z~l​ℓl​(z~l).d_{w}=-\ell_{w}^{\prime}(\tilde{z}_{w})=-\frac{\partial}{\partial\tilde{z}_{w}}\ell_{w}(\tilde{z}_{w}),\qquad d_{l}=\ell_{l}^{\prime}(\tilde{z}_{l})=\frac{\partial}{\partial\tilde{z}_{l}}\ell_{l}(\tilde{z}_{l}). (30)

Here ℓw\ell_{w} and ℓl\ell_{l} are outer shaping functions corresponding to zwz_{w} and zlz_{l}, respectively.

We now derive the incentive coefficients (dw,dl)(d_{w},d_{l}) for disentangled cases.

KTO.

KTO (Ethayarajh et al., 2024, Kahneman-Tversky optimization) applies pointwise shaping in log-probability space:

ℒKTO​(zw,zl)=λw​σ​(zwref−zw)+λl​σ​(zl−zlref).\mathcal{L}_{\text{KTO}}(z_{w},z_{l})=\lambda_{w}\sigma(z_{w}^{\text{ref}}-z_{w})+\lambda_{l}\sigma(z_{l}-z_{l}^{\text{ref}}). (31)

Let σ′​(u)≜σ⁡(u)​(1−σ⁡(u))\sigma^{\prime}(u)\triangleq\sigma(u)(1-\sigma(u)). Then

dw=λw​σ′​(zwref−zw)=λw​σ′​(−z~w),dl=λl​σ′​(zl−zlref)=λl​σ′​(z~l),d_{w}=\lambda_{w}\sigma^{\prime}\left(z_{w}^{\text{ref}}-z_{w}\right)=\lambda_{w}\sigma^{\prime}(-\tilde{z}_{w}),\qquad d_{l}=\lambda_{l}\sigma^{\prime}\left(z_{l}-z_{l}^{\text{ref}}\right)=\lambda_{l}\sigma^{\prime}(\tilde{z}_{l}), (32)

so KTO satisfies dw≠dld_{w}\neq d_{l} in general.

DDRO.

DDRO ((Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025), direct density ratio optimization) operates on an unpaired dataset introduced by KTO. The resulting objective of DDRO is defined as:

ℒDDRO​(zw,zl)=log⁡2−z~w+log⁡2−log⁡(2−ez~l),\mathcal{L}_{\text{DDRO}}(z_{w},z_{l})=\log 2-\tilde{z}_{w}+\log 2-\log\left(2-e^{\tilde{z}_{l}}\right), (33)

where ℓw​(z~w)=log⁡2−z~w\ell_{w}(\tilde{z}_{w})=\log 2-\tilde{z}_{w} and ℓl​(z~l)=log⁡2−log⁡(2−ez~l)\ell_{l}(\tilde{z}_{l})=\log 2-\log\left(2-e^{\tilde{z}_{l}}\right). Then, we have

dw=1,dl=ez~l2−ez~l.d_{w}=1,\qquad d_{l}=\frac{e^{\tilde{z}_{l}}}{2-e^{\tilde{z}_{l}}}. (34)
DIL-BCE.

The BCE (Hastie et al., 2001) variant in DIL (Xiao et al., 2025) is

ℒDIL-BCE​(zw,zl)=log⁡(1+e−z~w)+log⁡(1+ez~l).\mathcal{L}_{\text{DIL-BCE}}(z_{w},z_{l})=\log\left(1+e^{-\tilde{z}_{w}}\right)+\log\left(1+e^{\tilde{z}_{l}}\right). (35)

Using dd​u​log⁡(1+e−u)=−σ⁡(−u)\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}u}\log(1+e^{-u})=-\sigma(-u) and dd​u​log⁡(1+eu)=σ⁡(u)\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}u}\log(1+e^{u})=\sigma(u), we obtain

dw=σ⁡(−z~w),dl=σ⁡(z~l).d_{w}=\sigma(-\tilde{z}_{w}),\qquad d_{l}=\sigma(\tilde{z}_{l}). (36)
DIL-UKL.

The UKL (Nguyen et al., 2010) variant in DIL (Xiao et al., 2025) uses ℒDIL-UKL​(zw,zl)=ez~l−z~w\mathcal{L}_{\text{DIL-UKL}}(z_{w},z_{l})=e^{\tilde{z}_{l}}-\tilde{z}_{w}, yielding

dw=1,dl=ez~l.d_{w}=1,\qquad d_{l}=e^{\tilde{z}_{l}}. (37)
DIL-LSIF.

The LSIF (Kanamori et al., 2009) variant in DIL (Xiao et al., 2025) uses ℒDIL-LSIF​(zw,zl)=12​e2​z~l−ez~w\mathcal{L}_{\text{DIL-LSIF}}(z_{w},z_{l})=\frac{1}{2}e^{2\tilde{z}_{l}}-e^{\tilde{z}_{w}}, yielding

dw=ez~w,dl=e2​z~l.d_{w}=e^{\tilde{z}_{w}},\qquad d_{l}=e^{2\tilde{z}_{l}}. (38)

Appendix B Proofs

B.1 Proof of Sec. 3.2

See 3.2

Proof of Sec. 3.2.

Fix a time tt and consider the infinitesimal evolution induced by the local update direction at 𝜽t{\bm{\theta}}_{t}.

By the assumed differentiability of zw​(𝜽)z_{w}({\bm{\theta}}) and zl​(𝜽)z_{l}({\bm{\theta}}), first-order Taylor expansions around 𝜽t{\bm{\theta}}_{t} yield

zw,t+η\displaystyle z_{w,t+\eta} =zw,t+⟨∇𝜽zw​(𝜽t),𝜽t+η−𝜽t⟩+𝒪⁡(‖𝜽t+η−𝜽t‖2),\displaystyle=z_{w,t}+\left\langle\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}z_{w}({\bm{\theta}}_{t}),\ {\bm{\theta}}_{t+\eta}-{\bm{\theta}}_{t}\right\rangle+\mathcal{O}\left(\|{\bm{\theta}}_{t+\eta}-{\bm{\theta}}_{t}\|^{2}\right), (39)
zl,t+η\displaystyle z_{l,t+\eta} =zl,t+⟨∇𝜽zl​(𝜽t),𝜽t+η−𝜽t⟩+𝒪⁡(‖𝜽t+η−𝜽t‖2).\displaystyle=z_{l,t}+\left\langle\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}z_{l}({\bm{\theta}}_{t}),\ {\bm{\theta}}_{t+\eta}-{\bm{\theta}}_{t}\right\rangle+\mathcal{O}\left(\|{\bm{\theta}}_{t+\eta}-{\bm{\theta}}_{t}\|^{2}\right). (40)

Introduce the score vectors at time tt, 𝒔w|l,t≜∇𝜽zw|l​(𝜽t){\bm{s}}_{w|l,t}\triangleq\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}z_{w|l}({\bm{\theta}}_{t}). With this notation, the linear terms in Eqs. 39 and 40 become ⟨𝒔w,t,𝜽t+η−𝜽t⟩\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{\theta}}_{t+\eta}-{\bm{\theta}}_{t}\rangle and ⟨𝒔l,t,𝜽t+η−𝜽t⟩\langle{\bm{s}}_{l,t},{\bm{\theta}}_{t+\eta}-{\bm{\theta}}_{t}\rangle respectively. Consider a gradient descent discretization with step size η>0\eta>0,

𝜽t+η−𝜽t=−η​∇𝜽ℒ​(𝜽t)=η⁡(dw,t​𝒔w,t−dl,t​𝒔l,t),\displaystyle{\bm{\theta}}_{t+\eta}-{\bm{\theta}}_{t}=-\eta\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}\mathcal{L}({\bm{\theta}}_{t})=\eta\left(d_{w,t}{\bm{s}}_{w,t}-d_{l,t}{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\right), (41)

where the second equation can be derived by the unified gradient form evaluated at 𝜽t{\bm{\theta}}_{t}, −∇𝜽ℒ​(𝜽t)=dw,t​𝒔w,t−dl,t​𝒔l,t-\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}\mathcal{L}({\bm{\theta}}_{t})=d_{w,t}{\bm{s}}_{w,t}-d_{l,t}{\bm{s}}_{l,t}, as defined in Eq. 5. In particular, This implies ‖𝜽t+η−𝜽t‖=𝒪⁡(η)\|{\bm{\theta}}_{t+\eta}-{\bm{\theta}}_{t}\|=\mathcal{O}(\eta) as η→0\eta\to 0, so the Taylor remainders in Eqs. 39 and 40 satisfy 𝒪⁡(‖𝜽t+η−𝜽t‖2)=𝒪⁡(η2)\mathcal{O}(\|{\bm{\theta}}_{t+\eta}-{\bm{\theta}}_{t}\|^{2})=\mathcal{O}(\eta^{2}).

Substituting Eq. 41 into the linear terms in Eqs. 39 and 40 gives

zw,t+η−zw,t\displaystyle z_{w,t+\eta}-z_{w,t} =⟨𝒔w,t,η⁡(dw,t​𝒔w,t−dl,t​𝒔l,t)⟩+𝒪⁡(η2)\displaystyle=\left\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},\ \eta\left(d_{w,t}{\bm{s}}_{w,t}-d_{l,t}{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\right)\right\rangle+\mathcal{O}(\eta^{2})
=η⁡(dw,t​⟨𝒔w,t,𝒔w,t⟩−dl,t​⟨𝒔w,t,𝒔l,t⟩)+𝒪⁡(η2)\displaystyle=\eta\left(d_{w,t}\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\rangle-d_{l,t}\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\rangle\right)+\mathcal{O}(\eta^{2})
=η⁡(dw,t​‖𝒔w,t‖2−dl,t​⟨𝒔w,t,𝒔l,t⟩)+𝒪⁡(η2),\displaystyle=\eta\left(d_{w,t}\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|^{2}-d_{l,t}\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\rangle\right)+\mathcal{O}(\eta^{2}), (42)
zl,t+η−zl,t\displaystyle z_{l,t+\eta}-z_{l,t} =⟨𝒔l,t,η⁡(dw,t​𝒔w,t−dl,t​𝒔l,t)⟩+𝒪⁡(η2)\displaystyle=\left\langle{\bm{s}}_{l,t},\ \eta\left(d_{w,t}{\bm{s}}_{w,t}-d_{l,t}{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\right)\right\rangle+\mathcal{O}(\eta^{2})
=η⁡(dw,t​⟨𝒔l,t,𝒔w,t⟩−dl,t​⟨𝒔l,t,𝒔l,t⟩)+𝒪⁡(η2)\displaystyle=\eta\left(d_{w,t}\langle{\bm{s}}_{l,t},{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\rangle-d_{l,t}\langle{\bm{s}}_{l,t},{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\rangle\right)+\mathcal{O}(\eta^{2})
=η⁡(dw,t​⟨𝒔w,t,𝒔l,t⟩−dl,t​‖𝒔l,t‖2)+𝒪⁡(η2),\displaystyle=\eta\left(d_{w,t}\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\rangle-d_{l,t}\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|^{2}\right)+\mathcal{O}(\eta^{2}), (43)

where we used ⟨𝒔l,t,𝒔w,t⟩=⟨𝒔w,t,𝒔l,t⟩\langle{\bm{s}}_{l,t},{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\rangle=\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\rangle.

Divide Eqs. 42 and 43 by η\eta and take η→0\eta\to 0 to derive the instantaneous dynamics:

z˙w,t\displaystyle\dot{z}_{w,t} =limη→0zw,t+η−zw,tη=dw,t​‖𝒔w,t‖2−dl,t​⟨𝒔w,t,𝒔l,t⟩+limη→0𝒪⁡(η)=dw,t​‖𝒔w,t‖2−dl,t​⟨𝒔w,t,𝒔l,t⟩,\displaystyle=\lim_{\eta\to 0}\frac{z_{w,t+\eta}-z_{w,t}}{\eta}=d_{w,t}\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|^{2}-d_{l,t}\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\rangle+\lim_{\eta\to 0}\mathcal{O}(\eta)=d_{w,t}\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|^{2}-d_{l,t}\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\rangle, (44)
z˙l,t\displaystyle\dot{z}_{l,t} =limη→0zl,t+η−zl,tη=dw,t​⟨𝒔w,t,𝒔l,t⟩−dl,t​‖𝒔l,t‖2+limη→0𝒪⁡(η)=dw,t​⟨𝒔w,t,𝒔l,t⟩−dl,t​‖𝒔l,t‖2.\displaystyle=\lim_{\eta\to 0}\frac{z_{l,t+\eta}-z_{l,t}}{\eta}=d_{w,t}\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\rangle-d_{l,t}\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|^{2}+\lim_{\eta\to 0}\mathcal{O}(\eta)=d_{w,t}\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\rangle-d_{l,t}\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|^{2}. (45)

which are exactly Eq. 6. ∎

B.2 Proof of Sec. 3.2

See 3.2

Proof of Sec. 3.2.

By definition, mt=zw,t−zl,tm_{t}=z_{w,t}-z_{l,t}, hence m˙t=z˙w,t−z˙l,t\dot{m}_{t}=\dot{z}_{w,t}-\dot{z}_{l,t}. Substituting the dynamics in Eq. 6, we obtain

m˙t\displaystyle\dot{m}_{t} =(dw,t​‖𝒔w,t‖2−dl,t​⟨𝒔w,t,𝒔l,t⟩)−(dw,t​⟨𝒔w,t,𝒔l,t⟩−dl,t​‖𝒔l,t‖2)\displaystyle=\Bigl(d_{w,t}\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|^{2}-d_{l,t}\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\rangle\Bigr)-\Bigl(d_{w,t}\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\rangle-d_{l,t}\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|^{2}\Bigr)
=dw,t​‖𝒔w,t‖2+dl,t​‖𝒔l,t‖2−(dw,t+dl,t)​⟨𝒔w,t,𝒔l,t⟩.\displaystyle=d_{w,t}\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|^{2}+d_{l,t}\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|^{2}-(d_{w,t}+d_{l,t})\langle{\bm{s}}_{w,t},{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\rangle.

This finishes the proof. ∎

B.3 Proof of Sec. 3.2

See 3.2

Proof of Sec. 3.2.

Recall the DB written in log-ratio form:

log⁡‖𝒔l,t‖‖𝒔w,t‖+log⁡ρt≤log⁡rt≤log⁡‖𝒔l,t‖‖𝒔w,t‖−log⁡ρt.\log\frac{\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|}{\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|}+\log\rho_{t}\leq\log r_{t}\leq\log\frac{\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|}{\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|}-\log\rho_{t}. (46)

Define the two DB thresholds in ratio space as

at≜ρt​‖𝒔l,t‖‖𝒔w,t‖,bt≜1ρt​‖𝒔l,t‖‖𝒔w,t‖,a_{t}\triangleq\rho_{t}\frac{\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|}{\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|},\qquad b_{t}\triangleq\frac{1}{\rho_{t}}\frac{\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|}{\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|}, (47)

so that log⁡rt∈DB\log r_{t}\in\mathrm{DB} is equivalent to rt∈[at,bt]r_{t}\in[a_{t},b_{t}]. Let ct≜at​btc_{t}\triangleq\sqrt{a_{t}b_{t}}.

By definition,

Δt​(log⁡rt)=min⁡{log⁡rtat,log⁡btrt}.\Delta_{t}(\log r_{t})=\min\left\{\log\frac{r_{t}}{a_{t}},\log\frac{b_{t}}{r_{t}}\right\}. (48)
Inverval rt∈[at,ct]r_{t}\in[a_{t},c_{t}].

We first consider rt∈[at,ct]r_{t}\in[a_{t},c_{t}]. Since rt≤ctr_{t}\leq c_{t} and all quantities are positive,

rt≤at​bt\displaystyle r_{t}\leq\sqrt{a_{t}b_{t}} ⟹rt2≤at​bt⟹rtat≤btrt⟹log⁡rtat≤log⁡btrt.\displaystyle\Longrightarrow r_{t}^{2}\leq a_{t}b_{t}\Longrightarrow\frac{r_{t}}{a_{t}}\leq\frac{b_{t}}{r_{t}}\Longrightarrow\log\frac{r_{t}}{a_{t}}\leq\log\frac{b_{t}}{r_{t}}. (49)

The last implication uses that log⁡(⋅)\log(\cdot) is strictly increasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty). Therefore, on [at,ct][a_{t},c_{t}] the minimum in Eq. 48 is attained by the first term, namely Δt​(log⁡rt)=log⁡rtat\Delta_{t}(\log r_{t})=\log\frac{r_{t}}{a_{t}} for all rt∈[at,ct]r_{t}\in[a_{t},c_{t}].

Moreover, for any at≤rt<rt′≤cta_{t}\leq r_{t}<r_{t}^{\prime}\leq c_{t},

Δt​(log⁡rt′)−Δt​(log⁡rt)=log⁡rt′at−log⁡rtat=log⁡rt′rt>0,\displaystyle\Delta_{t}(\log r_{t}^{\prime})-\Delta_{t}(\log r_{t})=\log\frac{r_{t}^{\prime}}{a_{t}}-\log\frac{r_{t}}{a_{t}}=\log\frac{r_{t}^{\prime}}{r_{t}}>0, (50)

so Δt​(log⁡rt)\Delta_{t}(\log r_{t}) is strictly increasing on [at,ct][a_{t},c_{t}].

Inverval rt∈[ct,bt]r_{t}\in[c_{t},b_{t}].

Next consider rt∈[ct,bt]r_{t}\in[c_{t},b_{t}]. Since rt≥ctr_{t}\geq c_{t},

rt≥at​bt\displaystyle r_{t}\geq\sqrt{a_{t}b_{t}} ⟹rt2≥at​bt⟹rtat≥btrt⟹log⁡rtat≥log⁡btrt.\displaystyle\Longrightarrow r_{t}^{2}\geq a_{t}b_{t}\Longrightarrow\frac{r_{t}}{a_{t}}\geq\frac{b_{t}}{r_{t}}\Longrightarrow\log\frac{r_{t}}{a_{t}}\geq\log\frac{b_{t}}{r_{t}}. (51)

Hence, on [ct,bt][c_{t},b_{t}] the minimum in Eq. 48 is attained by the second term: Δt​(log⁡rt)=log⁡btrt\Delta_{t}(\log r_{t})=\log\frac{b_{t}}{r_{t}} for all rt∈[ct,bt]r_{t}\in[c_{t},b_{t}].

For any ct≤rt<rt′≤btc_{t}\leq r_{t}<r_{t}^{\prime}\leq b_{t},

Δt​(log⁡rt′)−Δt​(log⁡rt)=log⁡btrt′−log⁡btrt=log⁡rtrt′<0,\displaystyle\Delta_{t}(\log r_{t}^{\prime})-\Delta_{t}(\log r_{t})=\log\frac{b_{t}}{r_{t}^{\prime}}-\log\frac{b_{t}}{r_{t}}=\log\frac{r_{t}}{r_{t}^{\prime}}<0, (52)

so Δt​(log⁡rt)\Delta_{t}(\log r_{t}) is strictly decreasing on [ct,bt][c_{t},b_{t}].

Together, since Δt​(log⁡rt)\Delta_{t}(\log r_{t}) is strictly increasing on [at,ct][a_{t},c_{t}] and strictly decreasing on [ct,bt][c_{t},b_{t}], it has a unique maximizer on [at,bt][a_{t},b_{t}] at rt=ctr_{t}=c_{t}. Finally,

log⁡rt⋆=log⁡ct=12​(log⁡at+log⁡bt)=log⁡‖𝒔l,t‖‖𝒔w,t‖.\displaystyle\log r_{t}^{\star}=\log c_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\big(\log a_{t}+\log b_{t}\big)=\log\frac{\|{\bm{s}}_{l,t}\|}{\|{\bm{s}}_{w,t}\|}. (53)

This completes the proof.

Proof of Sec. 3.3.

Let sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}(\cdot) denote the stop-gradient operator: for any scalar xx, sg⁡(x)=x\operatorname{sg}(x)=x in the forward pass while ∂∂x​sg⁡(x)=0\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\operatorname{sg}(x)=0 in the backward pass.

Fix time tt. Let rt≜dw,t/dl,tr_{t}\triangleq d_{w,t}/d_{l,t} be the incentive ratio induced by the base objective ℒ⁡(zw,zl)\mathcal{L}(z_{w},z_{l}) at time tt, and let rt⋆r_{t}^{\star} be the target ratio in Sec. 3.2. Define

αt≜(rt⋆rt)1/2=exp⁡(12​(log⁡rt⋆−log⁡rt)).\alpha_{t}\triangleq\left(\frac{r_{t}^{\star}}{r_{t}}\right)^{1/2}=\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}(\log r_{t}^{\star}-\log r_{t})\right). (54)

We construct calibrated likelihoods by

zw,trc≜αt​zw,t+(1−αt)​sg⁡(zw,t),zl,trc≜αt−1​zl,t+(1−αt−1)​sg⁡(zl,t).z_{w,t}^{\rm rc}\triangleq\alpha_{t}z_{w,t}+(1-\alpha_{t})\operatorname{sg}(z_{w,t}),\qquad z_{l,t}^{\rm rc}\triangleq\alpha_{t}^{-1}z_{l,t}+(1-\alpha_{t}^{-1})\operatorname{sg}(z_{l,t}). (55)

By construction, in the forward pass we have zw,trc=zw,tz_{w,t}^{\rm rc}=z_{w,t} and zl,trc=zl,tz_{l,t}^{\rm rc}=z_{l,t}, but in the backward pass the Jacobians satisfy

∂zw,trc∂zw,t=αt,∂zl,trc∂zl,t=αt−1,∂zw,trc∂zl,t=∂zl,trc∂zw,t=0,\frac{\partial z_{w,t}^{\rm rc}}{\partial z_{w,t}}=\alpha_{t},\qquad\frac{\partial z_{l,t}^{\rm rc}}{\partial z_{l,t}}=\alpha_{t}^{-1},\qquad\frac{\partial z_{w,t}^{\rm rc}}{\partial z_{l,t}}=\frac{\partial z_{l,t}^{\rm rc}}{\partial z_{w,t}}=0, (56)

since ∂∂z​sg⁡(z)=0\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\operatorname{sg}(z)=0.

Now consider the composed objective ℒ⁡(zw,trc,zl,trc)\mathcal{L}(z_{w,t}^{\rm rc},z_{l,t}^{\rm rc}), viewed as a function of (zw,t,zl,t)(z_{w,t},z_{l,t}) through the transformations above, and define the calibrated incentive coefficients by the same rule:

dw,trc≜−∂ℒ⁡(zw,trc,zl,trc)∂zw,t,dl,trc≜∂ℒ⁡(zw,trc,zl,trc)∂zl,t.d_{w,t}^{\rm rc}\triangleq-\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}(z_{w,t}^{\rm rc},z_{l,t}^{\rm rc})}{\partial z_{w,t}},\qquad d_{l,t}^{\rm rc}\triangleq\phantom{-}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}(z_{w,t}^{\rm rc},z_{l,t}^{\rm rc})}{\partial z_{l,t}}. (57)

Applying the chain rule and using Eq. 56, we obtain

∂ℒ⁡(zw,trc,zl,trc)∂zw,t\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}(z_{w,t}^{\rm rc},z_{l,t}^{\rm rc})}{\partial z_{w,t}} =∂ℒ⁡(zw,trc,zl,trc)∂zw,trc⋅∂zw,trc∂zw,t+∂ℒ⁡(zw,trc,zl,trc)∂zl,trc⋅∂zl,trc∂zw,t=αt​∂ℒ⁡(zw,trc,zl,trc)∂zw,trc,\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}(z_{w,t}^{\rm rc},z_{l,t}^{\rm rc})}{\partial z_{w,t}^{\rm rc}}\cdot\frac{\partial z_{w,t}^{\rm rc}}{\partial z_{w,t}}+\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}(z_{w,t}^{\rm rc},z_{l,t}^{\rm rc})}{\partial z_{l,t}^{\rm rc}}\cdot\frac{\partial z_{l,t}^{\rm rc}}{\partial z_{w,t}}=\alpha_{t}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}(z_{w,t}^{\rm rc},z_{l,t}^{\rm rc})}{\partial z_{w,t}^{\rm rc}}, (58)
∂ℒ⁡(zw,trc,zl,trc)∂zl,t\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}(z_{w,t}^{\rm rc},z_{l,t}^{\rm rc})}{\partial z_{l,t}} =∂ℒ⁡(zw,trc,zl,trc)∂zw,trc⋅∂zw,trc∂zl,t+∂ℒ⁡(zw,trc,zl,trc)∂zl,trc⋅∂zl,trc∂zl,t=αt−1​∂ℒ⁡(zw,trc,zl,trc)∂zl,trc.\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}(z_{w,t}^{\rm rc},z_{l,t}^{\rm rc})}{\partial z_{w,t}^{\rm rc}}\cdot\frac{\partial z_{w,t}^{\rm rc}}{\partial z_{l,t}}+\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}(z_{w,t}^{\rm rc},z_{l,t}^{\rm rc})}{\partial z_{l,t}^{\rm rc}}\cdot\frac{\partial z_{l,t}^{\rm rc}}{\partial z_{l,t}}=\alpha_{t}^{-1}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}(z_{w,t}^{\rm rc},z_{l,t}^{\rm rc})}{\partial z_{l,t}^{\rm rc}}.

dl,trc\displaystyle d_{l,t}^{\rm rc} =∂ℒ⁡(zw,trc,zl,trc)∂zl,t=αt−1​∂ℒ∂zl,trc=αt−1​∂ℒ∂zl,t=αt−1​dl,t.\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}(z_{w,t}^{\rm rc},z_{l,t}^{\rm rc})}{\partial z_{l,t}}=\alpha_{t}^{-1}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z_{l,t}^{\rm rc}}=\alpha_{t}^{-1}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z_{l,t}}=\alpha_{t}^{-1}d_{l,t}.

Finally, letting rtrc≜dw,trc/dl,trcr_{t}^{\rm rc}\triangleq d_{w,t}^{\rm rc}/d_{l,t}^{\rm rc} and using Eq. 60, we have

rtrc=αt​dw,tαt−1​dl,t=αt2​dw,tdl,t=αt2​rt.r_{t}^{\rm rc}=\frac{\alpha_{t}d_{w,t}}{\alpha_{t}^{-1}d_{l,t}}=\alpha_{t}^{2}\frac{d_{w,t}}{d_{l,t}}=\alpha_{t}^{2}r_{t}.

Taking logs gives log⁡rtrc=log⁡rt+2​log⁡αt\log r_{t}^{\rm rc}=\log r_{t}+2\log\alpha_{t}. By the definition of αt\alpha_{t}, 2​log⁡αt=log⁡rt⋆−log⁡rt2\log\alpha_{t}=\log r_{t}^{\star}-\log r_{t}, hence

log⁡rtrc=log⁡rt⋆,\log r_{t}^{\rm rc}=\log r_{t}^{\star},
